items.why: Tests whether 'did not' governs reform or the renewed appointment of priests.
Attribution to the buried man matters, but the unnamed 'he' and 'message ... happen' make the question awkward.
Distinguishes Jonathan's single killing from the collective victory, though the final sentence supplies the answer directly.
Tracks the officer through the man of God's reply and the final pronoun identifying the trampling victim.
Singular 'he' and saddling the donkey 'for him' make the sons a weak rival for this minor action.
Tests the difference between the first covenant including the Lord and the separate king–people covenant.
Succession is easily guessed, and Isaiah's recording is not dated relative to the burial.
Separates the stated reason for Uzziah's own eagerness from the priests' simultaneous effort to remove him.
The capture-to-entry sequence is clear, but leaving camp is an easily rejected earlier step.
Distinguishes the rejected hypothetical trip into the city from the chosen plan to surrender at the camp.
Only narrative listing orders the two separate battles; which killing comes first is incidental.
'The news' supplies no content, and the Aramean camp is the topic of that very report.
The rival has the king order his own capture, which common sense rejects without resolving 'him'.
The question names Azariah among the followers, making him an implausible person for that same group to follow.
Requires mapping 'your son' and 'my son' through the woman's report before assigning today and tomorrow.
Separates Amaziah's example from Zechariah's teaching through the relative clause.
Distinguishes Elisha's answer to skepticism from his earlier price prophecy, both of which are declarations.
The rival treats a hypothetical half-share as an inadequate actual offer; the explicit divine command is much stronger.
Requires the eating–talking–departure sequence, but tests a relatively incidental final activity.
Mobilizing before marching and besieging follows ordinary military logic, so the rival needs little textual checking.
Separates Jehoiada's act of giving from David's former ownership of the weapons.
The accusers–council distinction matters, though the final sentence states the answer directly.
The rival answers cause rather than purpose, and 'take Amaziah's son' is an awkward formulation.
Requires resolving 'their command' to the family leaders rather than the earlier officials who mustered the army.
The departing traveler must remain distinct from the prophet who saddles the donkey, or the victim switches.
Requires tracking the officer through a clause about the king and into 'trampled him'.
Both on-duty and off-duty companies are joined as subjects of the order to guard the temple.
The salutation's 'To' identifies Felix as recipient without requiring substantial comprehension.
'The Philistine' identifies the victim, while rescuing David makes killing David an implausible alternative.
Separates a newly proposed report from earlier hiding, though admitting wrongdoing already favors the corrective action.
Separates Paul, who initiates the referral, from the young man identified by 'he' as having the message.
Requires keeping the messengers' return and report between their pursuit and the people's plundering.
'He loved the soil' contrasts singular Uzziah with plural workers, leaving a simple grammatical shortcut.
Requires linking 'my son' to the woman speaking to the king, not to the woman who hides her child.
The king's request and the repeated 'man of God interceded' make the praying agent easy to recover.
Distinguishes the peoples God helps Uzziah fight from the Ammonites who bring tribute.
The city and tomb are nested destinations, so 'first' tests a minor and somewhat artificial distinction.
The nurse phrasing points to Joash, while the passage already says Ahaziah is dead.
Tests the stated cause of the city's calm rather than treating the people's rejoicing as that cause.
Distinguishes the centurions receiving the preparation order from the soldiers they must prepare.
Distinguishes the kings hired to attack from the king believed to have hired them.
Identifies the murderer as the sender of the execution order, not the messenger sent to carry it out.
The final sentence explicitly names the eater, allowing readers to bypass the embedded claim's pronouns.
Lamps are not a plausible motive for prolonged speech, so common sense eliminates the rival.
The contrast between cavalry continuing and soldiers returning depends on tracking the two groups across pronouns.
Plural 'they' and the attacker–victim setup largely eliminate the single possessed man without tracing the full reference chain.
Cured illnesses can also be said to leave; distinguishing them from spirits relies on verb matching, not meaning.
Distinguishes the council petitioning for Paul's transfer from the commander asked to bring him.
Burning precedes valuation in the account, a sequence that cannot be safely guessed from usual practice.
Distinguishes the order to remove the woman from the conditional order to kill her followers.
Keeps the noise that prompts Athaliah's visit distinct from the sight she encounters after arriving.
The broad 'before the ambushers act' does not clearly exclude Paul's requested transfer as another prerequisite.
Speaker–addressee tracking is useful, but 'whose body is warned' is grammatically malformed.
Keeps the future son Josiah as the killer inside the prophecy rather than importing Jeroboam from the surrounding scene.
